items.title: SAG-Mem-1.0 Technical Report
items.summary: Long-term conversational memory requires retrieving complementary facts scattered across dialogue sessions, including intermediate evidence with limited similarity to the original question. Existing approaches often rely on derived memory representations or persistent relational structures, introducing construction costs and potentially losing source details. We present SAG-Mem, a conversational memory framework that preserves complete dialogue messages in non-overlapping chunks and discovers complementary evidence through query-time lexical expansion. Memory construction requires no model inference, using a lexical index without LLM-based extraction, summarization, or semantic relation construction. At query time, BM25 retrieves initial candidates, an evidence evaluator identifies useful chunks, and lexical cues from selected evidence guide an additional retrieval round. Retrieved dialogue is further annotated with calendar interpretations of supported relative-time expressions, preserving the original wording and temporal granularity. We also introduce SAG-Mem-Lite, an alternative configuration that replaces evidence scoring with embedding-based candidate scoring, achieving lower operational cost than Full Context and all memory-based baselines across both benchmarks with low query latency. On LoCoMo and LongMemEval, SAG-Mem achieves overall scores of 83.08 and 80.20, respectively, the highest among the evaluated methods on both benchmarks. On LongMemEval, it exceeds the strongest compared baseline by 7.20 points. SAG-Mem-Lite achieves scores of 77.09 and 77.20, respectively. These results support dialogue preservation and evidence-guided retrieval expansion as an effective design for long-term conversational memory.

items.title: Why Your Agent Needs Ambient Context, Not Just Skills | Birgitta Boeckeler, Unblocked
items.summary:
Everyone agrees context matters, but context isn't one thing. Birgitta Boeckeler, Principal Engineer & Developer Relations at Unblocked, separates codified context, like the AGENTS.md files and skills you deliberately author and reuse, from ambient context assembled at task time from Slack, wikis, tickets and PRs. She walks through what it takes to build a context engine that ingests, evaluates, assembles and observes ambient context, including how it resolves conflicting information using code as the source of reality. Recorded at AI DevCon New York 2026.

What we cover:
– Why 'context' needs more precise categories
– Codified vs ambient context, and why they're delivered differently
– A framework for what good-quality context looks like
– The limits of wiring agents to many MCP servers
– Building a context engine: ingest, evaluate, assemble, observe
– Resolving conflicting information, with code as the source of reality

Chapters:
00:00:00 - Introduction: context isn't one thing
00:02:20 - Codified vs ambient context
00:07:21 - A delivery lifecycle for context
00:08:37 - What good-quality context looks like
00:09:56 - Delivering ambient context with MCP servers
00:11:43 - Context engines
00:13:41 - Ingest: syncing many systems reliably
00:16:02 - Evaluating and assembling context
00:18:59 - Conflict detection: code as the source of reality
00:24:55 - Maintaining your context

items.title: Leto: Utility-Centric Agent Memory
items.summary: Large language model (LLM) agents rely on external memory to retain and reuse information across interactions. Existing memory systems treat memory as a record of the past and evaluate it by fidelity to the conversation. However, the value of memory lies in whether it improves the agent's response. A memory system decides what to memorize and what to serve before that response exists, and fidelity checks neither decision against it. Faithful memory can therefore fail to improve the response. We instead view memory as a prediction problem and present \textbf{\emph{\leto{}}}, a memory system for LLM agents that focuses on the utility of memory to the future rather than on its fidelity to the past. Because future requests are unknown, \emph{\leto{}} preserves access to conversation details through memory indexing, allowing information to remain available through its sources. When a request arrives, memory replay draws on this index to anticipate and supply the context the agent needs beyond what the request explicitly states. The utility of the served context remains uncertain until the response is generated, motivating a utility loop that uses response outcomes to refine future memory selection. We evaluate our system against six memory systems on five benchmarks across three scenarios. In personalization, it outperforms the strongest compared memory system by 16.3 percentage points in accuracy on PrefEval and by 3.1 points in task completion on PERMA. For long-horizon tasks, it achieves the best overall performance on MemoryArena averaged over five environments with a gain that increases with the chain depth. In long-context understanding, it is on par with retrieval over the raw history while serving fewer context tokens.

items.title: LEGOSpec: A Composable and Efficient Framework for Speculative Draft Design and Training
items.summary: Speculative decoding accelerates large language model (LLM) generation using a lightweight draft. Existing methods evaluate complete recipes under different training configurations, leaving component effects, interactions, and composition benefits unclear. Therefore, we present LEGOSpec, a composable framework for speculative draft design and training. LEGOSpec decomposes draft models into Context, Backbone, Proposal, and Objective components that share a unified training infrastructure. Using LEGOSpec, we systematically vary components and evaluate selected combinations under matched training conditions to isolate their effects and interactions. These experiments reveal three findings: (1) Different workloads favor different backbones, depending on context length and memory budget, with within-block dependency modeling particularly important for long contexts. (2) Proposal design must balance acceptance and latency. (3) The training objective should match token distributions locally and optimize acceptance length across the block. These findings guide workload-aware configurations and DFlux, a balanced general-purpose draft combining a convolution-equipped SWA--GQA hybrid backbone, Residual Corrector, and hierarchical supervision. Across Qwen and Gemma models, DFlux improves acceptance length over the strongest baseline by up to 13.7% on regular benchmarks and 34.7% on long-context workloads. To support efficient training, LEGOSpec integrates metadata-aware scheduling and asynchronous execution, increasing training throughput by up to 79% and accelerating offline supervision preparation by up to $3.11\times$ over SpecForge.

items.title: The Agent Lake
items.summary: An agent lake holds every trace your agents produce. See how LangSmith finds high-signal traces at scale and turns them into fixes and fine-tuned models.
items.content_excerpt: The trace of an agent is the system of record of what the agent did. It contains rich information about user intent, agent trajectory, and final outcome achieved. The simplest way to use these traces is as a debugging tool to visualize the sequence of steps an LLM application took and determine what went wrong. As agent traces become longer (as agents become more powerful) and more plentiful (as agents reach production), this manual debugging no longer scales. In order to use this trace data to drive continuous improvement of agents at scale, you need two things: We’ve been working on both of these for nearly two years. The first big piece we launched was SmithDB , a purpose-built database for traces. Over the past few months, we’ve been increasing our focus on “intelligent compute”. The reason you need “intelligent compute” is that these agent traces themselves are traces of unstructured reasoning, so intelligence is required to analyze them. In traditional data engineering, a data lake stores a shared corpus of data that different engines can query and process. As we’ve built LangSmith, we’ve noticed our platform architecture converging to that as well: a shared corpus of agent data (stored in SmithDB) with many different forms of “intelligent compute” running over it. Traditional data lakes like Snowflake and Databricks don’t have storage or “intelligent compute” optimized for this agent data. As more and more of the data a company generates becomes agent traces, we think it is important to develop this new type of platform. Most of what lands in the agent lake is traces. A trace records every step of an agent run, from the user’s input through each model call and tool call to the final output, and multi-turn conversations are grouped into threads so the whole interaction can be read together. Our agent lake, LangSmith, ingests traces from billions of agent runs per month. Some customers, like Clay, send us hundreds of millions of events per day. This kind of scale is why we built SmithDB , which is the industry’s most performant database specifically for real-time workloads on top of agent trace data. The agent lake also holds outcomes. Traces show you how the agent worked; outcomes show you the impact of that work. There are two dimensions on which to think about outcomes. First is how outcomes map to threads and/or traces . Some outcomes map 1-to-1 to a thread or trace. For example, a thumbs down on a trace means that agent response for that turn was

items.title: vLLM Day-0 Support for ERNIE 5.5 Flash Preview: Plugin Deployment and E2E Inference Acceleration
items.summary: vLLM supports Baidu's ERNIE 5.5 Flash Preview on day 0 through the vLLM-ERNIE plugin on the released vllm==0.32.0 wheel, with structure-aware kernel fusion, FlashIndexer, W4A8 QAT and DSpark speculative decoding.
items.story_key: model:vllm|ver:5.5|variant:flash,preview|title:vllm day 0 support for ernie 5 5 flash preview plugin deployment and e2e inferen
items.content_excerpt: The Baidu ERNIE team has worked with vLLM to bring day-0 support for ERNIE 5.5 Flash Preview to vLLM. ERNIE 5.5 Flash Preview is a sparse mixture-of-experts (MoE) model with 280B total parameters and 14B activated per token. It supports a 1M-token context, thinks before it answers, and uses tool calling to carry out long-horizon Agent tasks. vLLM supports the model on release day through the vLLM-ERNIE plugin, a standalone package that you install into the same environment as the official vllm==0.32.0 wheel. Install the released vLLM wheel and the plugin into the same environment. vLLM discovers the plugin automatically through its vllm.general_plugins entrypoint, so there is nothing to import or configure. The following command serves the default FP4 weights on a single 4-GPU node, with DSpark speculative decoding drafting 7 tokens per step: To turn off thinking for a request, pass "chat_template_kwargs": {"enable_thinking": false} . Launch commands for 1M context, attention TP and PD disaggregation are in the vLLM-ERNIE README and the vLLM recipe . ERNIE 5.5 Flash was designed with inference cost as a primary goal from the start, weighing activated compute, KV cache size and long-context overhead together. Every component, from the attention structure and residual connections to the MoE layers and the output head, was redesigned around that goal. For design and training details, see the ERNIE 5.5 Flash Preview blog . ERNIE 5.5 Flash introduces several new structures in attention and MoE: low-rank cross-head post-mixing (VHA post-mix), Multi-Router Latent MoE, the MultiMax output head and sigmoid output gating. When implemented op by op from their mathematical definitions, these structures produce many intermediate tensors and pay for them in memory traffic and kernel launches. For each structure, we designed a dedicated fused kernel around its compute and memory-access profile, and folded everything that can be precomputed into the weights at load time. The fused kernels run 1.55× to 6.53× faster than naive implementations. Together, these fusions cover the full forward pass of ERNIE 5.5 Flash, from attention and MoE routing to the output head. They cut the number of kernel launches and the round trips of intermediate tensors through GPU memory while keeping the numerics aligned, and they underpin the model's high inference performance. The Baidu ERNIE inference team developed FlashIndexer, a lightweight indexer acceleration built on dynamic head routing

items.title: claude-code v2.1.332
items.summary:
What's changed

  • Added skills from MCP servers (beta). They show as server:skill in the / menu; other skills keep their names
  • Added a PreSkillShellCommand hook event that can refuse a skill or command's inline shell commands as it loads; on 2.1.331 and older, a settings file naming it opens a dialog at start
  • Added "Always deliver" to the prompt for held messages from other sessions
  • Added a footer line that stays while a flagged message has your session on a different model, until you pick one with /model
  • Added an OpenTelemetry assistant_response event for text Claude sends through SendUserMessage or Cowork's message tool, when response logging is on
  • Added a warning in VS Code and Desktop's Code tab when part of a session couldn't be saved, saying how to save it with /compact
  • Added a notice in VS Code and Desktop's Code tab when a resumed session's earlier messages weren't loaded, as the terminal already shows
  • Added your Cyber Verification Program access tier to the startup header, beside the model name when your tier applies to that model and you're signed in with a claude.ai account
  • Fixed claude auth login reporting Login successful. when a claude.ai login could not be saved: it now exits 1 and says what to check, such as a leftover lock file or a full disk
  • Fixed Read, @-mentions and compaction hanging on a named pipe that nothing writes to, such as a .env mounted by a locked secrets manager; the read now fails after 20 seconds
  • Fixed turns ending in "Prompt is too long" after repeated auto-compaction failures when one more compaction at the context limit could have kept them going
  • Fixed compaction failing when a summary kept running past the output limit: after three cut-off replies, the last try now asks for a shorter summary
  • Fixed a freeze when a permission rule or hook condition with several wildcards was checked against a long command
  • Fixed freezes and runaway memory use in most cases while a hook prints output without end
  • Fixed a freeze and context overflow when a hook blocks or fails during a turn, or after /compact, with a very large log; text over about 50,000 characters is now shortened
  • Fixed the terminal freezing, and ignoring Ctrl+C, while a local MCP server floods its standard output
  • Fixed a freeze when a prompt or piped input holds an @ followed by a very long unbroken string, such as minified CSS with an embedded font
  • Fixed a long freeze when opening a rewind point after a large tracked file was rewritten
  • Fixed SSE MCP servers hanging or refusing every tool call after their event stream was cut and came back on a new endpoint or not at all, until reconnected by hand
  • Fixed Remote Control showing a session in the desktop app, VS Code or the Agent SDK as running while it waited there on a dialog or an MCP server's question
  • Fixed a usage limit being reported as reached to Remote Control, IDE and SDK clients after it had already reset
  • Fixed CLAUDE.md and rules files being sent to the model a second time, in most cases, after a session moves into a worktree under .claude/worktrees with EnterWorktree or is resumed there
  • Fixed tool calls that never ran being counted as done in a claude.ai chat's summary line after you declined a permission prompt in a session that had restarted
  • Linux: Fixed the Bash edit diff showing an unchanged symlink as edited after Claude had read the file through it
  • Fixed resuming a session and /stats freezing for seconds when a transcript holds many damaged lines
  • Fixed a family name such as sonnet in --fallback-model being dropped when availableModels allows only an older version of it
  • Fixed keys lagging for seconds while /stats reads large session transcripts, also after the dialog is closed, and with debug logging on while a language server floods its stderr
  • Fixed a session failing when the cloud refused its default model and an availableModels list that isn't enforced named neither it nor an older model of that family
  • Fixed an enforced list of older models failing on Google Cloud's Agent Platform and Foundry when the first is refused: it now steps down to the next in that family, if listed newest first
  • Fixed opus failing on Bedrock, Google Cloud's Agent Platform and Foundry behind a gateway that refuses a model in its own words: it now steps down to an older model that answers
  • Fixed the start-up model upgrade offer on Bedrock and Google Cloud's Agent Platform naming a model that your availableModels list leaves out
  • Fixed Bedrock sub-agents failing when your account lists no profile for their model in the parent's region: they now use the model's own profile, which can be outside that region
  • Fixed Foundry sessions leaving a model family when an admin's list blocks the version sonnet, opus or haiku points to: they now use its newest allowed version under a built-in or mapped name
  • Fixed the sonnet alias on Bedrock Mantle resolving to Haiku 4.5: it now means Sonnet 5, not Sonnet 5.5, and an account without Sonnet 5 gets an error, so enable it first
  • Fixed Ctrl+C at the prompt starting a new turn, and a double Ctrl+C not exiting, when a background agent it stopped had an unread subagent report
  • Fixed /install-github-app ticking a workflow again after going back with Esc
  • Fixed dictated text past 10,000 characters being lost
  • Fixed raw "JSON Parse error" and "The operation was aborted." API errors when the non-streaming retry got a broken response or was interrupted
  • Fixed Esc not stopping computer use between actions on macOS when Claude Code's window or an app you allowed is in front; an Esc meant for that app's popup now stops computer use instead
  • Fixed a rare hang when a helper command, such as an API key helper, ran past its time limit
  • Fixed selecting text in fullscreen pushing the footer's right-hand label onto a second row, which moved the text under the mouse and could copy the wrong line
  • Fixed a PreToolUse hook's reason for asking not showing on terminal Read, Grep, Glob, Edit and Write prompts (#102892, #105343)
  • Fixed temp_* folders piling up in ~/.claude/plugins/cache when a downloaded plugin couldn't be copied into place

  • Fixed headless and cloud sessions reporting a foreground fork's Agent call as finished the moment the fork started

  • Fixed idle compaction being skipped for subscribers still well under their weekly limit

  • Fixed a resumed conversation sometimes missing its last messages after a crash or kill on Bedrock, Google Cloud's Agent Platform, Foundry and other third-party providers
  • Fixed NotebookEdit saving an invalid notebook when an edit changes a cell's type; turning a cell with attachments into code is now refused
  • Fixed a long README in a design system moved from standalone Claude Design losing its list of files to load when Claude starts a deck or design
  • Fixed MCP tool calls failing with "malformed task handle" when the server's task ID is longer than 128 characters; IDs of up to 1,024 characters now work

  • Fixed stale and repeated rows in the fullscreen Ctrl+R history picker when prompts share a timestamp
  • Fixed Code Mode silently skipping a tool call whose input has a list of over 4,096 items, and freezing on a very large typed array in a tool's input, which is now refused
  • Fixed Code Mode leaving a message unanswered when it was typed during a command and Esc was pressed before Claude replied; the message now starts a new turn, which a second Esc stops
  • Fixed Code Mode not telling Claude when a slow command moved to the background and left its script with empty output, or of the time limit on background commands in claude -p and the Agent SDK
  • Fixed Code Mode sometimes waiting for minutes on a command that had already been stopped
  • Fixed a typed slash command's inline shell commands not running in Code Mode after a background script's output arrived
  • Fixed Code Mode sessions in the Agent SDK and claude -p sometimes losing Claude's last reply on resume after being stopped while a script was running
  • Remote Control: Fixed sessions hosted by the desktop app or VS Code showing as idle while /compact runs
  • Fixed a session sometimes losing its "needs input" status after a background task's report in Claude Desktop
  • Fixed Grep: -o missing an empty match at the end of a file with no last newline, -o with multiline adding an empty line or misnumbering lines in non-UTF-8 files, and -A and -B ignored beside a zero -C
  • Fixed unbinding a chord in keybindings.json still leaving its first key waiting for a second when it was spelled meta and bound as alt, or the reverse
  • Fixed moving an empty session to the background sometimes failing with "Couldn't load transcript from file"
  • Fixed OpenTelemetry reporting a failed mcp_server_connection event at each start for a built-in server that isn't turned on for the account
  • Fixed Esc not stopping a Bash command while it waited for its file diff in large or slow git repositories, which held the next message
  • Fixed pasted links and relative paths ending in an image file name appearing late and swallowing an Enter pressed right after
  • Fixed /mcp reconnect all and /mcp disable all counting a built-in server that isn't turned on for the account
  • Fixed interrupting a turn while a mod's turn.step hook was waiting showing "user-cancel" as an error instead of "Interrupted"
  • Fixed ~/.claude.json being reported as corrupted when another session was in the middle of saving it
  • Fixed web searches failing with an API error when Claude's list of allowed or blocked domains was empty or had duplicates
  • Fixed resuming a paused workflow in Code Mode waiting for minutes while other background work was running
  • Fixed subagents in Code Mode failing with "Agent stalled" and losing their command when a script ran for more than 10 minutes
  • Improved claude plugin marketplace add on Windows to wait and try again in some cases when another program, such as a virus scanner, briefly holds the downloaded files
  • Windows: Improved stability on some company PCs, where Claude Code could exit with no output shortly after start
  • Improved computer use setup: the Screen Recording permission prompt can now restart Claude Code and resume the chat
  • Improved computer use to take less context until Claude uses it
  • Improved the error when a proxy or gateway cuts or damages a compressed response: a turn now ends in plain words instead of raw "ZlibError fetching" text
  • Improved /context: shorter output in fullscreen, so the total is less likely to scroll off in a short window, and the legend names its unit once

items.title: How the Claude Code team thinks about verification
items.summary: How end-to-end, property and differential tests let coding agents verify their work with evidence, and what the Claude Code team does to keep its verifiers honest.
items.story_key: model:claude code|title:how the claude code team thinks about verification
items.content_excerpt: How end-to-end, property and differential tests let coding agents verify their work with evidence, and what the Claude Code team does to keep its verifiers honest. On the Claude Code team, the vast majority of our code (~90%) is written and reviewed by Claude . At this scale, how we equip our agents to verify their work with evidence becomes extremely important. Verification loops are the building block that lets you delegate more work to Claude. Without them, you can really only run one or two Claudes at a time, because you have to check everything yourself. With them, you can run dozens or hundreds in parallel. That’s because giving agents a way to verify their output is an effective way to improve quality. In internal testing around structured file generation, having a separate grader check Claude’s work against a rubric improved task success by up to 10 points over a standard prompting loop, with the largest gains on the hardest problems. What was once expensive to verify (tests, benchmarks, specs, real end-to-end runs) is now cheap to request from an agent. Like code, agents can quickly generate tests, benchmarks, and specs. And once generated, these tests and benchmarks run as software so they can be run frequently without using many additional tokens. You can also close the verification loop by using the results to improve the agent’s performance on that task. For example, if an agent repeatedly fails a test that checks logs for user data, you can create a hook or a more explicit rule in your CLAUDE.md to avoid future issues. This (mostly) stops issues from happening again. So if verification is critical to producing quality code at a high velocity, what types of tests should you use and how should you apply them across your pipeline? This article answers those questions and also shares the process used by the Claude Code team. If your tests are flaky you’ll train the agent to run them again rather than fixing the failing code. If your tests are slow, the agent will do fewer tests across batches which can make pinpointing issues difficult. Heavier tests are best deployed before you’ve committed the changes. If you have to focus on one test type, pick end-to-end. These tests describe real user flows like adding an item to a cart, checking out, and moving to a confirmation page. The reason E2E tests are so effective is that they are difficult to fool–either the whole feature works or it doesn't. They also have definitive done criteria and can concrete

items.story_key: model:claude|title:using a chaos loop to harden the claude docs launch 60 server errors across bill
items.content_excerpt: Claude Docs is a doc editor that you, your teammates, and Claude all work in together. The interesting part is that a Claude session anywhere, from chat to Claude Code, can open the same doc and read, write, and comment in it live, right next to you. We released Docs on September 16, 2026. This post is about the service that runs underneath it. Three weeks before Claude Docs opened to the public, it was running as a proof of concept on a single node, used by a few thousand people inside Anthropic. We were racing toward an ambitious launch date, and our own estimate said we'd see millions of docs within the first few days. We launched on September 16. By September 22, people had created over 4.6 million docs. Across 2 billion requests we saw only 60 server errors, and we never had to roll back. The whole Docs service ran on about 50 memory-optimized pods. But honestly, this only worked because our frontier models have gotten much better recently (I used an internal research model roughly comparable to Claude Fable 5.2). In our experience, they can now stick with one goal through a run like this for weeks, which is what helped us hit launch scale in a tight timeline. A few thousand internal users on one machine told us nothing about whether the service would survive launch, and we obviously didn't have launch traffic to test with. We wanted real evidence to decide how fast we could roll out. So on September 4, about two weeks before launch, I had Claude drive a staging cluster that mirrored production at over a million synthetic docs a day and break core components on purpose. And then... I just left it running (I've included the full cost at the end of this article). My setup was pretty simple. The loop was a session in Claude Code that I left running: pick a scenario, run the harness, read the telemetry, propose a fix, ship it to staging, repeat. That session acted as a coordinator and handed most of the work to sub-agents. In the busiest week, that usually meant about 11 sub-agents running at a time, and 30 at the peak. The coordinator also talked to our internal variant of Claude Tag (beta) via the Slack MCP to learn from other infrastructure teams at Anthropic who had scaled similar services. Their agents checked our scaling approach for pitfalls they’d already hit. Each iteration looked the same. items.title: Data + AI Anywhere: AlloyDB Omni integration with local models
items.summary:
Open models like Gemma 4 from Google DeepMind are a great option to keep your data local. But how can a local AI model integrate with on-premises data?

AlloyDB Omni, Google’s 100% PostgreSQL-compatible database that runs anywhere, now integrates with locally hosted large language models (LLMs). With AlloyDB Omni, you can build agentic experiences on your own infrastructure and on your own terms. Whether it’s in the cloud, in your datacenter, or even on your laptop, you can have data plus AI anywhere.

Built-in AI for your local environment

AlloyDB Omni is a downloadable, run-anywhere edition of AlloyDB that easily deploys to your own infrastructure, including on-premises. AlloyDB Omni packs powerful, built-in AI, including the same ScaNN indexing technology powering Google Search. When you pair AlloyDB Omni with a model, you can store vector embeddings at scale; search them semantically; and even query the database using natural language. You can use virtually any model you like, whether that’s a frontier Cloud-hosted model like Gemini or a local model. And with locally hosted models you maintain complete control over your data environment.

Connecting to Gemma 4, Qwen3.8, and other local models

You can now connect AlloyDB Omni to local models like Gemma 4 and Qwen3.8. No matter which model you choose, the architecture remains the same.

This setup enables entirely new use cases for environments that were previously blocked from adopting agentic capabilities. If you operate an air-gapped network or have data locality requirements, you can still build intelligent applications. You can analyze local logs, generate summaries of proprietary internal documents, and power localized chatbots—all while maintaining strict data governance.

  • Keep data on-premises: Because the database and the model sit in the same local environment, your data never crosses the public internet.

  • Reduce latency: Processing inference requests locally minimizes network transit time.

  • Query directly via SQL: Your standard database queries can invoke machine learning functions that process data locally. Like this:

code_block
<ListValue: [StructValue([('code', "SELECT customer_name, ai.generate('Summarize in 1 short sentence: ' || comment, model_id => 'gemma4_llm') AS summary FROM customer_feedback; customer_name | summary ---------------+----------------------------------------------------------------------- Alice | The customer demands a refund for a double charge or they will cancel Bob | The user likes the product but requests dark mode support."), ('language', ''), ('caption', <wagtail.rich_text.RichText object at 0x7fccb8104110>)])]>

Next, you’ll see how to run queries like this yourself, step by step.

Get started

You can test this integration on your own machines today. Using a Kubernetes environment we will show you how to deploy and integrate AlloyDB Omni and a local open model.

Step 0: Before you begin

In this example, we will use Google Kubernetes Engine (GKE) to host the AlloyDB Omni database and local model. GKE gives us a standardized, reproducible environment but you can use the same setup on-prem or almost anywhere.

We will assume you have already setup:

  1. A GKE cluster, and

  2. Kubernetes tools kubectl and Helm

Step 1: Deploy the AlloyDB Omni Kubernetes Operator

We will use the AlloyDB Omni Kubernetes operator to set up our AlloyDB Omni database. The Operator makes deploying and maintaining AlloyDB Omni a breeze.

code_block
<ListValue: [StructValue([('code', "helm install \ cert-manager oci://quay.io/jetstack/charts/cert-manager \ --version v1.21.3 \ --namespace cert-manager \ --create-namespace \ --set crds.enabled=true \ --set global.leaderElection.namespace=cert-manager helm install alloydbomni-operator oci://gcr.io/alloydb-omni/alloydbomni-operator \ --version 1.9.0 \ --create-namespace \ --namespace alloydb-omni-system \ $(helm install --help | grep -q -- '--rollback-on-failure' && echo '--rollback-on-failure' || echo '--atomic') \ --timeout 5m"), ('language', ''), ('caption', <wagtail.rich_text.RichText object at 0x7fccb8106f90>)])]>

Step 2: Create your AlloyDB Omni database

Don’t forget to enable the googleMLExtension.

code_block
<ListValue: [StructValue([('code', 'kubectl create namespace ai-demo cat << \'EOF\' | kubectl apply -f - apiVersion: v1 kind: Secret metadata: name: db-pw-my-omni namespace: ai-demo type: Opaque data: my-omni: "VmVyeVN0cm9uZ1Bhc3N3b3Jk" # password "VeryStrongPassword" --- apiVersion: alloydbomni.dbadmin.goog/v1 kind: DBCluster metadata: name: my-omni namespace: ai-demo spec: databaseVersion: "18.4.0" primarySpec: adminUser: passwordRef: name: db-pw-my-omni features: googleMLExtension: enabled: true resources: cpu: 2 memory: 4Gi disks: - name: DataDisk size: 20Gi storageClass: standard dbLoadBalancerOptions: annotations: networking.gke.io/load-balancer-type: "internal" allowExternalIncomingTraffic: true EOF'), ('language', ''), ('caption', <wagtail.rich_text.RichText object at 0x7fccb8106b90>)])]>

Step 3: Deploy your AI model

We will use Ollama to help us deploy our model.

In this example we deploy Gemma 4 from Google DeepMind. Or, you can modify this command to deploy Qwen3.8 – just change a few lines as noted in the comments.

code_block
<ListValue: [StructValue([('code', 'cat << \'EOF\' | kubectl apply -f - apiVersion: apps/v1 kind: Deployment metadata: name: ollama namespace: ai-demo spec: replicas: 1 selector: matchLabels: app: ollama template: metadata: labels: app: ollama spec: containers: - name: ollama image: ollama/ollama:latest ports: - containerPort: 11434 env: - name: OLLAMA_KEEP_ALIVE value: "-1" # keep the model in RAM - name: OLLAMA_LOAD_TIMEOUT value: "20m" resources: requests: cpu: "4" memory: "16Gi" # for Qwen 3.8: 24Gi volumeMounts: - name: models mountPath: /root/.ollama lifecycle: postStart: exec: command: ["/bin/sh", "-c", "(sleep 5 && ollama pull gemma4:12b) >/dev/null 2>&1 &"] # For Qwen 3.8, comment out the line above and use this one: # command: ["/bin/sh", "-c", "(sleep 5 && ollama pull qwen3.8) >/dev/null 2>&1 &"] volumes: - name: models ephemeral: volumeClaimTemplate: spec: accessModes: ["ReadWriteOnce"] resources: requests: storage: 30Gi --- apiVersion: v1 kind: Service metadata: name: ollama-service namespace: ai-demo spec: type: ClusterIP ports: - port: 11434 targetPort: 11434 selector: app: ollama EOF'), ('language', ''), ('caption', <wagtail.rich_text.RichText object at 0x7fccb85ebad0>)])]>

Step 4: Register the model with AlloyDB Omni

Connect to your database.

code_block
<ListValue: [StructValue([('code', 'kubectl exec -it -n ai-demo $(kubectl get pod -n ai-demo -l alloydbomni.internal.dbadmin.goog/task-type=database -o jsonpath=\'{.items[0].metadata.name}\') -c database -- env PGPASSWORD="VeryStrongPassword" psql -h 127.0.0.1 -U postgres'), ('language', ''), ('caption', <wagtail.rich_text.RichText object at 0x7fccb85eb190>)])]>

Note: If you receive a connection error, you might need to wait a moment for your database to provision.

Now you should be connected to your AlloyDB Omni database with the psql client. Next, run the following SQL script to register your local model.

code_block
<ListValue: [StructValue([('code', "CREATE EXTENSION IF NOT EXISTS google_ml_integration; ALTER SYSTEM SET google_ml_integration.request_timeout_in_seconds = 600; SELECT pg_reload_conf(); CREATE OR REPLACE FUNCTION google_ml.ollama_llm_input_transform( model_id character varying, prompt text, generation_config json, system_instructions json ) RETURNS json AS $$ SELECT json_build_object( 'model', CASE model_id WHEN 'gemma4_llm' THEN 'gemma4:12b' WHEN 'qwen3_8_llm' THEN 'qwen3.8' END, 'messages', json_build_array( json_build_object('role', 'system', 'content', COALESCE(system_instructions->'systemInstruction'->'parts'->0->>'text', 'You are a helpful assistant.')), json_build_object('role', 'user', 'content', prompt) ) ); $$ LANGUAGE sql; CREATE OR REPLACE FUNCTION google_ml.ollama_llm_output_transform( model_id character varying, response json ) RETURNS text AS $$ SELECT trim(regexp_replace( response->'choices'->0->'message'->>'content', '<think>.*?</think>', '', 's')); $$ LANGUAGE sql; CALL google_ml.create_model( model_id => 'gemma4_llm', -- and/or 'qwen3_8_llm', model_request_url => 'http://ollama-service.ai-demo.svc.cluster.local:11434/v1/chat/completions', model_provider => 'custom', model_type => 'llm', model_in_transform_fn => 'google_ml.ollama_llm_input_transform', model_out_transform_fn => 'google_ml.ollama_llm_output_transform' );"), ('language', ''), ('caption', <wagtail.rich_text.RichText object at 0x7fccb981cf90>)])]>

Note: If you receive a Resource not found error, wait a moment for the model to load.

In addition to registering your model, the above script tells AlloyDB Omni how to interpret the model’s raw output. In this example chain-of-thought (CoT) reasoning is part of the response inside <think></think> tags. We don’t want the CoT, so our output transform function removes it.

Step 5: Try it out!

You can use functions like ai.generate built-in to AlloyDB Omni to connect to your local model – without ever leaving the SQL client!

code_block
<ListValue: [StructValue([('code', "CREATE TABLE customer_feedback ( id SERIAL PRIMARY KEY, customer_name TEXT, comment TEXT ); INSERT INTO customer_feedback (customer_name, comment) VALUES ('Alice', 'I was charged twice on my credit card! Please refund $49 immediately or I will cancel.'), ('Bob', 'Great product, but can you please add dark mode support?'); SELECT customer_name, ai.generate('Summarize in 1 short sentence: ' || comment, model_id => 'gemma4_llm' /* or 'qwen3_8_llm' */) AS summary FROM customer_feedback;"), ('language', ''), ('caption', <wagtail.rich_text.RichText object at 0x7fccaab01690>)])]>

Make it your own

Try out all the AI features that AlloyDB Omni has to offer! AlloyDB Omni supports fast vector search, built-in AI functions, and more. Give them a try and build something great.

items.title: Lazy Agents Answer Against Their Own Beliefs: Reinforcement Learning with Verifiable Beliefs Teaches Them to Act on What They Believe
items.summary: AI agents working on long tasks often commit to an answer before they have enough evidence, a behavior called laziness. In our evaluations, they frequently commit even while their stated belief still names several possible answers. An outcome reward at the end of the episode scores only the final answer, so it cannot teach the agent when to commit, because a lucky guess receives the same reward as an answer backed by evidence. During training, however, the simulator can compute the exact posterior over the answer at every step and tell whether the evidence is already enough. We propose Reinforcement Learning with Verifiable Beliefs (RLVB), which rewards the agent for taking further steps while this posterior still allows several answers and for committing once the evidence is sufficient. The reward needs no judge, critic or reward model, and it never reads the belief line the agent writes before each action. We also introduce Pro Worlds, a benchmark of visual puzzles where the agent views a large world through a small window. We evaluate three vision-language models on three benchmarks, two of which are never seen in training. RLVB improves the base model in all nine settings, by 17.1% on average. Under the outcome reward, GRPO and PPO fall below the base model on average. RLVB also outperforms PPO with a process reward from an LLM judge by 9.3% on average while using 1.6 times fewer GPU-hours. The trained agent answers with sufficient evidence in 51%, 12% and 74% of the episodes on the three benchmarks, against 8%, 0.4% and 36% for the base model. Its accuracy gain therefore comes from answering more often at high levels of evidence. The belief line shows how the agent reaches this evidence: it acts on its own belief. It commits at only 0.1 to 2.2% of the turns at which the evidence is insufficient and its line still names several answers, against 3 to 68% for the base model.

items.title: ReQOR: Operator-Discrepancy Subspace Repair for Quantization-Conditioned Backdoors in Large Language Models
items.summary: Quantization-Conditioned Backdoors (QCBs) cause large language models (LLMs) to exhibit malicious behavior after quantization while remaining benign at high precision. Existing defenses often rely on security-guided configuration selection or iterative optimization, but do not identify which quantization-induced changes should be repaired. We isolate module-local quantization effects from upstream drift by evaluating the high-precision and quantized versions of each module on identical states from the quantized inference trajectory, and formulate QCB defense as repairing the resulting same-state operator discrepancies. We propose ReQOR, a training-free defense that identifies the dominant directions of these discrepancies on benign calibration data and restores the full-precision computation along them in closed form, yielding a factorized residual adapter. ReQOR uses neither attack information nor gradient-based optimization and supports both full-span and low-rank repair. Experiments across four LLMs, three PGD-based QCB attacks, three malicious behaviors, and three quantization formats show substantial QCB mitigation while largely preserving benign utility. In additional experiments on a non-PGD outlier-injection attack, existing baselines largely fail, whereas ReQOR remains effective. Further analysis shows that dominant operator-discrepancy directions provide more effective and rank-efficient repair than rank-matched random, low-energy, or raw weight-error directions, while low-rank ReQOR reduces deployment memory overhead.

items.title: Release 2.75.0 corresponding to NGC container 26.11
items.summary:
Triton Inference Server

The Triton Inference Server provides a cloud inferencing solution optimized for both CPUs and GPUs. The server provides an inference service via an HTTP or GRPC endpoint, allowing remote clients to request inferencing for any model being managed by the server. For edge deployments, Triton Server is also available as a shared library with an API that allows the full functionality of the server to be included directly in an application.

New Features and Improvements

  • PyTorch backend: Added AOTI BF16 input/output support.
  • THIRD-PARTY-NOTICES.txt is now included in the containers.
  • Fixed a use-after-free in the dynamic batcher and a preserve_ordering completion-slot issue on response-cache hits.
  • Prevented silent gRPC stream cancellations under backpressure.
  • Bounded the decompressed HTTP inference response size in the client library.
  • Perf Analyzer: Honored supplied output shapes, propagated the binary exit code, tagged the wheel as platform-specific, and limited profile-data export to the needed inputs and outputs.
  • Python backend: Now logs when the backend stub exits on a crash signal.

Known Issues

  • The Triton TensorRT-LLM Backend container image is not included in this release.
  • vLLM's v0 API and Ray are affected by vulnerabilities. Users should consider their own architecture and mitigation steps which may include but should not be limited to:
    • Do not expose Ray executors and vLLM hosts to a network where any untrusted connections might reach the host.
    • Ensure that only the other vLLM hosts are able to connect to the TCP port used for the XPUB socket. Note that the port used is random.
  • When using Valgrind or other leak detection tools on AGX-Thor or DGX-Spark systems, you might see memory leaks attributed to NvRmGpuLibOpen.
  • Valgrind or other memory leak detection tools may occasionally report leaks related to DCGM. These reports are intermittent and often disappear on retry.
  • CuPy has issues with the CUDA 13 Device API in multithreaded contexts. Avoid using tritonclient cuda_shared_memory APIs in multithreaded environments until fixed by CuPy.
  • TensorRT calibration cache may require size adjustment in some cases, which was observed for the IGX platform.
  • The core Python binding may incur an additional D2H and H2D copy if the backend and frontend both specify device memory to be used for response tensors.
  • A segmentation fault related to DCGM and NSCQ may be encountered during server shutdown on NVSwitch systems. A possible workaround for this issue is to disable the collection of GPU metrics tritonserver --allow-gpu-metrics false ....
  • When using TensorRT models, if auto-complete configuration is disabled and is_non_linear_format_io:true for reformat-free tensors is not provided in the model configuration, the model may not load successfully.
  • When using Python models in decoupled mode, users need to ensure that the ResponseSender goes out of scope or is properly cleaned up before unloading the model to guarantee that the unloading process executes correctly.
  • Triton Inference Server with vLLM backend currently does not support running vLLM models with tensor parallelism sizes greater than 1 and the default "distributed_executor_backend" setting when using explicit model control mode. In attempt to load a vllm model (tp > 1) in explicit mode, users could potentially see failure at initialize step: could not acquire lock for <_io.BufferedWriter name='<stdout>'> at interpreter shutdown, possibly due to daemon threads. For the default model control mode, after server shutdown, vllm related sub-processes are not killed. Related vllm issue: vllm-project/vllm#6766. Please specify "distributed_executor_backend":"ray" in the model.json when deploying vllm models with tensor parallelism > 1.
  • When loading models with file override, multiple model configuration files are not supported. Users must provide the model configuration by setting parameter "config" : "<JSON>" instead of custom configuration file in the following format: "file:configs/<model-config-name>.pbtxt" : "<base64-encoded-file-content>".
  • TensorRT-LLM backend provides limited support of Triton extensions and features.
  • The TensorRT-LLM backend may core dump on server shutdown. This impacts server teardown only and will not impact inferencing.
  • The Java CAPI is known to have intermittent segfaults.
  • Some systems which implement malloc() may not release memory back to the operating system right away causing a false memory leak. This can be mitigated by using a different malloc implementation. Tcmalloc and jemalloc are installed in the Triton container and can be used by specifying the library in LD_PRELOAD. NVIDIA recommends experimenting with both tcmalloc and jemalloc to determine which one works better for your use case.
  • Auto-complete may cause an increase in server start time. To avoid a start time increase, users can provide the full model configuration and launch the server with --disable-auto-complete-config.
  • Auto-complete does not support PyTorch models due to lack of metadata in the model. It can only verify that the number of inputs and the input names matches what is specified in the model configuration. There is no model metadata about the number of outputs and datatypes. Related PyTorch bug: pytorch/pytorch#38273
  • Triton Client PIP wheels for ARM SBSA are not available from PyPI and pip will install an incorrect Jetson version of Triton Client library for Arm SBSA. The correct client wheel file can be pulled directly from the Arm SBSA SDK image and manually installed.
  • Traced models in PyTorch seem to create overflows when int8 tensor values are transformed to int32 on the GPU. Refer to pytorch/pytorch#66930 for more information.
  • Triton cannot retrieve GPU metrics with MIG-enabled GPU devices.
  • Triton metrics might not work if the host machine is running a separate DCGM agent on bare-metal or in a container.

Client Libraries and Examples

The client libraries and examples are available in this release exclusively via the Ubuntu 24.04–based NGC Container. The SDK container includes the client libraries and examples, Performance Analyzer, and Model Analyzer. See Getting the Client Libraries for more information.

ManyLinux Assets (early access)

This release was compiled with AlmaLinux 8.9 based out of manylinux_2_34 and can be used on RHEL 9 and later versions.
See the included README.md for complete details about installation, verification, and support.
This release supports ensembles. Confirm CUDA, TensorRT, ONNX Runtime, PyTorch, and Python versions in the shipped README.md.
Some optional backend features such as the PyTorch backend's TorchTRT extension are not currently supported.
